deck: Consumer Goods in 2026 is a sector split down the middle: staples brands grinding through tariffs, affordability pressure, and private-label competition while identity-driven companies — in smoke-free nicotine, accessible beauty, off-price retail, and franchise IP — are growing with real pricing power and volume momentum.
summary:
The Consumer Goods sector in 2026 is not a single story. It is at least four stories running simultaneously, and the gap between them is widening. At the top, Philip Morris International is executing a once-in-a-generation category migration: smoke-free products now generate 41.5% of its $40B+ revenue base, adjusted EPS hit $7.54 in 2025, and the company added 4.5 million new smoke-free users in a single year. Coca-Cola posted $47.9B in revenue with zero-sugar variants growing 14% and a FIFA World Cup campaign that collected 25 million first-party data records. These are legacy companies with renewed structural momentum. In adjacent categories, e.l.f. Beauty delivered its 30th consecutive quarter of sales growth at 83% gross margin, Tapestry's Coach brand grew 31% with 35% of new customers being Gen Z, and Burlington Stores hit 6% comp growth in Q1 2026 while opening new stores at acceleration pace. The winning formula across this tier is the same: direct-to-consumer control, identity attachment, and the ability to serve value-seeking consumers without surrendering brand equity.

The struggling half of the sector is getting squeezed from multiple directions at once. Kraft Heinz saw 2025 organic net sales down 3.4% and is now committing $700M to repair brand relevance it should never have let erode. Whirlpool is cutting dividends, raising equity, and watching North American appliance demand hit recession-level lows while simultaneously absorbing resumed promotions that undercut a 10%-plus price increase taken in the same quarter. The Campbell's Company is running negative organic sales guidance for FY2026 even with Rao's pasta sauce surpassing $1B in trailing twelve-month revenue. Coty withdrew its full-year guidance entirely in February 2026 after geopolitical shock hit Middle East beauty markets and Consumer Beauty kept declining. The pattern is structural, not cyclical: consumers at the mid-market and below are under real affordability pressure, and they are trading down to private label, off-price, and value formats faster than incumbent brands can offset with volume.

The cross-sector tension is tariffs. Almost every company in this set — from toy makers to apparel brands to appliance manufacturers to beauty conglomerates — is reporting material tariff cost exposure, with China-sourced supply chains particularly exposed. Some companies (Tapestry, JAKKS Pacific, Spin Master, Funko, Build-A-Bear) received large one-time tariff refunds in Q1 or Q2 2026 that are masking underlying profitability. Others are absorbing $20M to $100M in incremental costs without equivalent pricing cover. The sector's earnings quality in 2026 is significantly noisier than headline numbers suggest because of these distortions. Companies with the cleanest paths forward are those with DTC-led channel mix, strong brand heat in identity or functional categories, geographic diversification outside North America, and at least partial domestic production — a short list that does not include most traditional packaged-goods incumbents.

sub_trends.name: Smoke-free category migration
sub_trends.what: Philip Morris International is executing the clearest large-scale consumer-category migration in the sector: shifting habitual nicotine demand from combustibles to IQOS, ZYN, and smoke-free pouches. Smoke-free is already 41.5% of revenue and growing 12.8% in volume, while combustibles still grew 9.5% in net revenue — both engines running simultaneously. The business model depends on addiction stickiness enabling pricing power during the transition, which is why the margin arithmetic looks better than any traditional consumer goods company.

sub_trends.name: Accessible beauty as share-gain machine
sub_trends.what: e.l.f. Beauty, Tapestry, and Victoria's Secret are each proving that accessible or aspirational-adjacent brands can compound market share when they execute on identity, community, and Gen Z cultural alignment. e.l.f. has delivered 30 consecutive quarters of growth at 83% gross margin. Tapestry's Coach acquired 2.2M new customers with 35% Gen Z mix. Victoria's Secret hit 13% comp growth in Q1 2026 after years of brand repair. The common thread is treating the product as a cultural signal, not a commodity purchase.

sub_trends.name: Off-price and closeout retail acceleration
sub_trends.what: Burlington and Ollie's Bargain Outlet are both growing comp sales and accelerating store openings in an environment where traditional retailers are pulling back. Burlington hit 6% comp growth in Q1 2026 and added 40 new stores in the quarter. Ollie's Army grew 12% to 17.5M members without a subscription fee. The macro is their tailwind: consumer affordability pressure pushes traffic directly into off-price formats where brand-name discovery at reduced prices is the product.

sub_trends.name: IP-driven franchise flywheels replacing toy retail
sub_trends.what: Hasbro and Mattel are both pivoting from toy-box category dependence to IP-led franchises that monetize across tabletop, digital, film, and collectibles simultaneously. Hasbro's Wizards of the Coast and Digital Gaming grew 45% in 2025, with Magic: The Gathering up 59% and Monopoly Go! contributing $168M annually. Mattel's Masters of the Universe movie released in Q2 2026 and action figures grew 35% in the same quarter. Physical product margins are under tariff and input-cost pressure; the real upside is IP licensing and digital monetization.

sub_trends.name: DTC channel capture as margin and data engine
sub_trends.what: Across apparel (Levi's, YETI, Abercrombie, lululemon), beauty (Tapestry, e.l.f.), and footwear (Crocs, Deckers), direct-to-consumer is the margin expansion lever. Levi's DTC reached 49% of revenue with Q2 gross margin at 62.7%. YETI's DTC is 60% of sales. Crocs' DTC grew 12% in Q2 2026. The shift is also a data capture story: owning the customer relationship means owning the purchase data, loyalty, and repeat-order economics that wholesale can never provide.

sub_trends.name: Staples brand repair under affordability and private-label pressure
sub_trends.what: Kraft Heinz, General Mills, Kimberly-Clark, Campbell's, and Colgate-Palmolive are all navigating the same problem: organic growth stuck in low single digits or negative territory, private-label competition persistent, and consumer price sensitivity preventing full tariff and input cost pass-through. Kraft Heinz is spending $700M to reinvest in brand relevance; General Mills is framing FY2027 around a 'step change in remarkability'; Campbell's organic net sales guidance is negative for FY2026. The era of passive pricing defense is over for this cohort.

standout_companies.why_notable: The cleanest large-scale category migration in consumer goods: smoke-free products already 41.5% of $40B+ revenue with 43M+ consumers using smoke-free formats, adjusted EPS nearly doubled from $4.52 to $7.54 in two years, and both combustibles and smoke-free grew simultaneously in 2026.

30 consecutive quarters of growth, 83% gross margin, and 7 consecutive years of market share gains in accessible beauty — the only company in this sector set that is compounding both volume and margin expansion simultaneously through social commerce and community-driven product drops.

Customer deposits hit an all-time high of $9.0B in Q2 2026 with 85% of 2026 capacity already booked and double-digit 2027 bookings growth, while also absorbing 30% higher fuel costs and Middle East conflict disruption — the best real-time demand signal in the sector.

Wizards of the Coast and Digital Gaming grew 45% in 2025 driven by Magic: The Gathering +59%, proving that a traditional toy company can convert IP into a software-economics franchise with recurring digital revenue at scale — Monopoly Go! alone contributed $168M annually.

Comp growth accelerated from Q3 2025 to Q4 to Q1 2026 (+2% to +4% to +6%) while simultaneously opening 40 new stores in a single quarter — a pure store-based, no-subscription off-price model executing at a moment when most retail formats are contracting.

Coach revenue grew 31% in Q3 2026 at 75% gross margin while acquiring 2.2M new customers with 35% Gen Z mix, demonstrating that accessible luxury with brand heat can gain share even in a tariff-pressured, affordability-sensitive consumer environment.

The FIFA World Cup campaign across 180+ markets collected 25M first-party data records from 80M consumer engagements via connected packaging — showing that a 130-year-old beverage brand can operate as a first-party data platform at scale while Zero Sugar grew 14% and Q2 2026 EPS grew 16%.

The clearest cautionary case: three years of under-investment resulted in organic net sales down 3.4% in 2025 and forced a $700M brand reinvestment commitment — a textbook example of how passive pricing strategy destroys consumer goods franchises.

tension: The sector's deepest fault line is the affordability-versus-identity split, and tariffs are the accelerant. Every company in this set is absorbing materially higher input costs from tariffs and commodity inflation. Companies with brand heat in identity-coded categories (accessible luxury, beauty, smoke-free nicotine, off-price discovery) can either hold pricing or route around affordability pressure through channel mix. Staples incumbents with household-necessity positioning cannot: private label is an adequate substitute, and consumers at the mid-market and below are making the substitution in real time. The second fault line is tariff accounting noise: multiple companies received large one-time refunds in Q1-Q2 2026 (Funko $25.4M, Spin Master $37.9M, JAKKS Pacific $11.1M, Build-A-Bear $7M) that make quarterly earnings look better than the underlying operating model justifies. When those refunds stop flowing, the underlying cost structure becomes visible and several companies currently reporting positive quarters will face a reckoning.
who_wins_who_loses: Winners are companies with identity-attached demand that survives affordability pressure (e.l.f. Beauty, Tapestry, Philip Morris, Deckers, Crocs), operators with DTC channel control that captures both margin and customer data (Levi's, YETI, Victoria's Secret), off-price retailers with treasure-hunt mechanics that benefit directly from consumer trade-down (Burlington, Ollie's), and IP-holding franchises that monetize across physical and digital formats simultaneously (Hasbro, Mattel). Losers are mid-market staples brands that allowed brand equity to erode through years of passive pricing (Kraft Heinz, General Mills in certain categories), single-channel electronics hardware manufacturers facing market saturation with no recurring revenue (GoPro), discretionary categories dependent on housing-cycle sentiment (Whirlpool), and any company with heavy China sourcing concentration and no DTC pricing buffer to absorb tariff pass-through. The department store middle is also a structural loser: Nordstrom went private to escape the pressure, and Macy's is surviving on media-network revenue and credit-card income rather than merchandise margin.
outlook: The Consumer Goods sector is bifurcating permanently, not temporarily. The macro pressure — tariffs, commodity inflation, consumer affordability constraint, private-label competition — does not go away when sentiment eventually improves because private-label penetration earned during a downturn tends to stick. Companies that have built identity, direct-channel relationships, and recurring digital touchpoints will continue to gain share regardless of the cycle. The next 12-18 months will clarify which staples incumbents can complete brand repair (Kraft Heinz's $700M bet and General Mills' FY2027 'remarkability' push are tests of this) and which are in secular decline. Tariff accounting distortions will fade, and the real cost structures of China-exposed hardware and toy companies will become visible. Philip Morris's smoke-free migration is the most compelling long-duration story in the sector: by the time smoke-free products reach 50-55% of revenue, the company will have effectively transformed its demand base without losing the cash engine. The companies that survive and compound are those that own the customer identity, control the distribution, and have a recurring reason to return beyond the household necessity cycle.
one_sentence: Consumer Goods in 2026 is a sector where identity-attached brands with direct-channel control are widening their lead while traditional staples incumbents discover that passive pricing cannot substitute for brand equity they spent a decade eroding.
